title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini Robotics 2 with whole-body humanoid control
subtitle: The three-model suite adds torso-to-legs coordination, on-device adaptation to new robot bodies, and an embodied-reasoning model for multi-robot planning.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google DeepMind released Gemini Robotics 2 on July 30 — a three-model suite consisting of a vision-language-action model for whole-body humanoid control, an embodied-reasoning model (Gemini ER 2) for multi-step planning and multi-robot collaboration, and an on-device variant designed to adapt to new robot morphologies within hours rather than weeks. The company reports a 92% success rate on unscrewing a light bulb, a task that requires coordinated torso, arm, and grip control at the same time. DeepMind is opening a waitlist for developers and has named Apptronik, Agile Robots SE, and Boston Dynamics as launch partners.

The step up from the 2025 release is whole-body coordination. The prior Gemini Robotics model handled arm-and-gripper tasks on a fixed base — pick, place, wipe, rearrange — but did not plan movement that had to travel down through the torso and legs. Whole-body control is the difference between a robot that can manipulate objects on a table and a robot that can lean into a task, brace against a surface, or step and reach in one continuous motion. That is the gap between what the industry has shipped for warehouses and what humanoids need to do in a house or a hospital.

This release sits in a broader race with Figure, Tesla Optimus, and China's Booster and BYD Xiao Di programs, all pushing on the same problem from the hardware side. DeepMind's angle is model-portability: the on-device variant is meant to transfer across robot bodies without retraining a foundation model from scratch, which — if it holds up — pulls the industry closer to the pattern that worked for language models. One capable base model, many downstream deployments, and a shrinking gap between the demo video and the production floor.

For learners: robotics has historically resisted the pattern that made LLMs suddenly useful — one big model, many downstream tasks — because every robot body was different and every environment broke transfer. Watch whether Gemini Robotics 2's on-device adaptation actually works across the three partner platforms. If it does, robotics stops being a bespoke systems-integration business and starts to look like the software-platform pattern that made cloud AI cheap enough to build companies on.
